note: Topic codes, titles, unit structure, HL-only flags and teaching hours are factual features of the syllabus. All study content (essentials, diagrams, traps) is EconIB original writing.

units.title: Introduction to economics
units.blurb: Why economics exists as a subject: resources are limited, so every choice costs something else.
covers: Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost
The production possibilities curve
Factors of production and the circular flow
Positive versus normative statements
The nine key concepts
units.why: Two topics, ten hours, and almost no exam questions of its own — but the language here appears in every answer you write for the next two years. Opportunity cost and the positive/normative distinction turn up in Paper 1 evaluation constantly.

units.title: Microeconomics
units.blurb: How individual markets set prices and quantities, and what happens when they get it wrong.
covers: Demand, supply and equilibrium
Elasticity: PED, YED and PES
Government intervention: taxes, subsidies, price controls
Market failure: externalities, public goods, common pool resources
HL only: asymmetric information, market power, equity
units.why: The biggest unit and the one most IA commentaries are written about, because news articles about prices are everywhere. Nearly every diagram you must be able to draw lives here.

units.title: Macroeconomics
units.blurb: The economy as a whole: output, jobs, prices, and what governments can do about them.
covers: Measuring activity: GDP, GNI, real versus nominal
Aggregate demand and aggregate supply
Unemployment, inflation and the objectives that conflict
Inequality, poverty and the Lorenz curve
Monetary, fiscal and supply-side policy
units.why: Where evaluation marks are won. Almost every policy has a cost, a time lag and a group who loses — say which, and you are in the top band.

units.title: The global economy
units.blurb: Trade between countries, exchange rates, and why some economies develop and others do not.
covers: Comparative advantage and the gains from trade
Protection: tariffs, quotas, subsidies
Economic integration and the WTO
Exchange rates and the balance of payments
Development: measuring it, barriers to it, strategies for it
units.why: The most current unit — trade disputes and exchange rate moves are in the news every week, which makes it the easiest place to find a genuinely recent IA article.

topics.title: What is economics?
essentials: Scarcity: finite resources against unlimited wants, which forces the three basic questions — what to produce, how, and for whom.
Opportunity cost as the value of the next best alternative forgone.
Factors of production: land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship, and the income each earns (rent, wages, interest, profit).
The production possibilities curve: points on it are efficient, inside are unemployed resources, outside are unattainable; the curve's shape shows increasing opportunity cost.
Economic systems: free market, planned, and mixed — and where real economies sit between them.
The circular flow of income between households and firms, with injections and leakages.
diagrams: Production possibilities curve, including a shift outward for growth
topics.trap: Opportunity cost is the NEXT BEST alternative forgone, singular — not the sum of everything you gave up.

terms.definition: The condition in which economic resources are limited relative to society's unlimited wants.
The value of the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made.
The resources used to produce goods and services: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship.
A curve showing the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce when all resources are fully and efficiently employed.
An economic system in which resources are allocated by the price mechanism with minimal government intervention.

lesson: Economics starts from one awkward fact: there is not enough of anything to go round. Not enough land, hours, machines or trained people to satisfy everything everyone wants. That is scarcity, and it is not a temporary problem to be solved — it is the permanent condition that makes the subject necessary.

Because resources are scarce, every choice is also a refusal. Use a field for housing and you cannot use it for farming. The value of the best thing you gave up is the opportunity cost, and it is what economists mean by the real cost of anything. Note the wording: the NEXT BEST alternative, not the sum of everything forgone.

The production possibilities curve draws this. Every point on the curve uses all resources efficiently; inside it, something is idle or wasted; outside it is currently impossible. The curve bows outward because resources are not equally good at both jobs — move a specialist chip factory to making burgers and you lose a lot of chips for very few burgers. That is increasing opportunity cost, and it is why the line curves rather than running straight.

topics.title: How do economists approach the world?
essentials: Economics as a social science: models simplify by holding other things constant (ceteris paribus).
Positive statements (testable against evidence) versus normative statements (value judgments about what ought to be).
The nine key concepts as the conceptual thread running through the whole course.
Different schools of thought disagree about how markets self-correct, which is why evaluation is possible at all.
Equity and sustainability as central lenses on modern economic problems.
topics.trap: 'The government should raise the minimum wage' is normative. 'Raising the minimum wage above equilibrium creates a surplus of labour' is positive. Examiners ask you to distinguish these.

terms.definition: The assumption that all other variables are held constant while the effect of one variable is examined.
A statement about what is, which can in principle be tested against evidence.
A statement about what ought to be, based on a value judgment and not testable by evidence.
A simplified representation of economic behaviour that isolates the relationships being studied.

lesson: Economics is a social science, which means it studies people who do not behave like billiard balls. To get anywhere, economists build models — deliberate simplifications that hold everything else still while they examine one relationship. That assumption has a name you must use: ceteris paribus, other things equal.

The distinction that earns marks is between positive and normative. A positive statement claims something about the world that could in principle be tested: raising interest rates reduces investment. A normative statement contains a value judgment: the government SHOULD raise interest rates. Watch for should, ought, fair and too much — they signal that someone has smuggled a preference in as a fact.

This matters because most policy questions are a mix of both, and the top evaluation marks go to answers that separate them. You can be certain about a mechanism and still disagree about whether it is worth doing.

topics.title: Demand
essentials: The law of demand: as price rises, quantity demanded falls, ceteris paribus.
Why the demand curve slopes down: income effect, substitution effect, and the law of diminishing marginal utility.
Non-price determinants: income, tastes and preferences, prices of substitutes and complements, expectations, number of consumers.
Movement ALONG the curve is caused by price; a SHIFT of the curve is caused by everything else.
Individual demand versus market demand as the horizontal sum.
diagrams: Movement along versus shift of the demand curve
hl: Assumptions behind the law of demand, including diminishing marginal utility
Linear demand functions: Qd = a - bP, and plotting them
topics.trap: 'Demand fell' and 'quantity demanded fell' are different claims. Price changes never shift the demand curve. This single confusion costs more marks than any other in Unit 2.

terms.definition: The quantity of a good consumers are willing and able to buy at each price over a given period.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, ceteris paribus.
A good that can be consumed in place of another, so a rise in the price of one raises demand for the other.
A good consumed together with another, so a rise in the price of one lowers demand for the other.
A good for which demand rises as consumer income rises.
A good for which demand falls as consumer income rises.

lesson: Demand is not desire. It is the quantity people are both willing AND able to buy at each price. Wanting a Ferrari is not demand; wanting one with the money to pay is.

The demand curve slopes down for two reasons worth naming. The income effect: when a price falls, your money goes further, so you can buy more. The substitution effect: when a price falls relative to alternatives, the good becomes better value and people switch to it.

Now the distinction that costs more marks than any other in this course. A change in the good's OWN price moves you ALONG the curve — that is a change in quantity demanded. A change in anything else — income, tastes, the price of a substitute, expectations, the number of buyers — SHIFTS the whole curve, and that is a change in demand. If you write that a price rise reduced demand, you have said the wrong thing, and an examiner will take the mark.

topics.title: Supply
essentials: The law of supply: as price rises, quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
Non-price determinants: costs of factors of production, prices of related goods (joint and competitive supply), indirect taxes and subsidies, expectations, technology, number of firms.
Movement along versus shift, exactly as with demand.
Individual firm supply versus market supply.
diagrams: Movement along versus shift of the supply curve
hl: The law of diminishing marginal returns and increasing marginal costs as the reason supply slopes up
Linear supply functions: Qs = c + dP
topics.trap: An indirect tax shifts supply LEFT (or upward by the tax per unit) — it is a cost to the producer, not a change in demand.

terms.definition: The quantity of a good producers are willing and able to sell at each price over a given period.
As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus.
Where producing one good automatically produces another, so a rise in output of one raises supply of the other.
A payment from government to producers that lowers their costs and increases supply.
A tax on expenditure, paid to government by the producer, which raises costs and reduces supply.

lesson: Supply is the quantity producers are willing and able to sell at each price. It slopes upward, and the reason is worth knowing rather than asserting: as a firm pushes output higher with a fixed factory, each extra unit costs more to make. Higher prices are needed to make that extra production worth doing.

The shift rule mirrors demand exactly. Price changes move you along the curve. Everything else shifts it: the cost of factors of production, technology, the number of firms, expectations, and taxes or subsidies.

Indirect taxes and subsidies are the two that appear constantly. A tax is a cost to the producer, so supply shifts left, or upward by the tax per unit. A subsidy lowers costs, so supply shifts right. Students routinely draw a tax as a demand shift, which turns the whole answer into the wrong story.

topics.title: Competitive market equilibrium
essentials: Equilibrium where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied; excess demand (shortage) below it and excess supply (surplus) above it.
How shifts in demand or supply produce a new equilibrium price and quantity.
Functions of the price mechanism: signalling, incentive, and rationing.
Consumer surplus, producer surplus, and social (community) surplus.
Allocative efficiency at the competitive equilibrium: community surplus is maximised where marginal benefit equals marginal cost.
diagrams: Changes in equilibrium and the price mechanism at work
hl: Calculating consumer and producer surplus from a diagram
Solving for equilibrium algebraically from demand and supply functions
topics.trap: Allocative efficiency is MB = MC, not simply 'where the curves cross'. State the condition; the free mark is in the wording.

terms.definition: The price and quantity at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is no tendency to change.
A shortage arising when price is below equilibrium and quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
A surplus arising when price is above equilibrium and quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.
The difference between what consumers are willing to pay and what they actually pay.
The difference between the price producers receive and the minimum they would accept.
The outcome where resources produce the combination of goods most wanted by society, achieved where marginal benefit equals marginal cost.

lesson: Equilibrium is the price at which the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. Nothing is left over, nobody is turned away, and there is no pressure on price to move. That last clause is the definition — equilibrium is not where the lines happen to cross on your paper, it is where the market has no reason to change.

Away from it, the market pushes back. Above equilibrium, supply exceeds demand and unsold stock forces sellers to cut prices. Below it, buyers compete for too few goods and price is bid up. That self-correcting movement is the price mechanism, and it does three jobs: it signals where resources are wanted, it gives an incentive to move them there, and it rations what is scarce.

At the competitive equilibrium something stronger is true. Consumer surplus and producer surplus together — community surplus — are at their maximum, and marginal benefit equals marginal cost. That is allocative efficiency. Say the condition, not just the word.

topics.title: Critique of the maximizing behaviour of consumers and producers
essentials: The rational consumer assumption of standard theory: perfect information, utility maximisation, consistent preferences.
Behavioural critiques: biases and rules of thumb, bounded rationality, bounded self-control, imperfect information.
Choice architecture and nudge theory as policy tools.
Firms may pursue objectives other than profit maximisation — market share, growth, corporate social responsibility, satisficing.
topics.trap: This topic is a gift for evaluation anywhere in the course. If a question assumes rational behaviour, questioning that assumption is a legitimate and well-credited evaluative move.

terms.definition: The idea that decision-makers have limited information and limited capacity to process it, so they satisfice rather than optimise.
The way choices are presented, which influences the decisions people make.
A change to choice architecture that alters behaviour predictably without forbidding options or changing incentives significantly.
A firm's pursuit of social and environmental objectives alongside, or instead of, profit maximisation.

lesson: Standard theory assumes people are rational: they have full information, know their own preferences, and choose whatever maximises their satisfaction. It is a useful assumption because it makes prediction possible. It is also, plainly, not true.

Behavioural economics catalogues the ways it fails. People have bounded rationality — limited information and limited capacity to process it, so they use rough rules rather than optimising. They have bounded self-control, choosing what feels good now over what serves them later. They are influenced by how a choice is presented, not just what it contains.

That last point is choice architecture, and it gives governments a cheap policy tool. Making pension enrolment the default rather than an opt-in raises saving dramatically without banning anything or changing a single price. Firms too may not maximise profit: they may pursue market share, growth, or corporate social responsibility. Whenever a question assumes rational behaviour, questioning that assumption is legitimate, well-credited evaluation.

topics.title: Elasticity of demand
essentials: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price; interpret the value, ignoring the negative sign.
Ranges: elastic (>1), inelastic (<1), unit elastic (=1), and the perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic extremes.
Determinants of PED: number and closeness of substitutes, degree of necessity, proportion of income spent, time.
PED and total revenue: raising price raises revenue when demand is inelastic and cuts it when elastic.
YED = % change in quantity demanded / % change in income; positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods, above 1 for luxuries.
Applications: why primary commodity producers face volatile incomes, and why the primary sector shrinks as economies develop.
diagrams: Relatively elastic and relatively inelastic demand
Perfectly elastic, perfectly inelastic and unit elastic demand
hl: PED varies along a straight-line demand curve — it is not constant
Engel curves for income elastic, income inelastic and inferior goods
Calculating PED and YED from data
topics.trap: PED is not the slope. A single straight demand curve has elastic, unit elastic and inelastic sections. Saying 'the flatter curve is more elastic' is only true when comparing at the same price and quantity.

terms.definition: The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price, measured as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.
Demand where PED is greater than one, so quantity demanded changes proportionately more than price.
Demand where PED is less than one, so quantity demanded changes proportionately less than price.
The responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in income, measured as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income.
Price multiplied by quantity sold.

lesson: Elasticity answers a question the demand curve alone cannot: not which way quantity moves, but by how much. Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Ignore the minus sign and read the size.

Above one, demand is elastic: quantity responds proportionately more than price. Below one it is inelastic: quantity barely moves. What decides it is mostly substitutes. Fuel has few, so demand is inelastic; one brand of crisps has many, so demand is elastic. Necessity, the share of income spent, and time all matter too — almost everything is more elastic in the long run, once people can adjust.

The practical payoff is revenue. If demand is inelastic, raising price raises total revenue, because quantity falls proportionately less. If it is elastic, raising price cuts revenue. This is why governments tax fuel and tobacco, and why a struggling restaurant discounting may be doing exactly the right thing.
One warning: PED is not the slope. A single straight demand curve is elastic at the top, unit elastic in the middle and inelastic at the bottom.

topics.title: Elasticity of supply
essentials: PES = % change in quantity supplied / % change in price.
Determinants: time, mobility of factors of production, spare capacity, ability to store stock, and the length of the production period.
Primary commodities tend to have low PES; manufactured goods higher.
diagrams: Relatively elastic and relatively inelastic supply
Perfectly elastic and perfectly inelastic supply
hl: Calculating PES from data
topics.trap: Time is the dominant determinant. Almost all supply is more elastic in the long run, and saying so is an easy evaluation point in any tax or subsidy question.

terms.definition: The responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price, measured as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.
Unused productive capability that allows a firm to raise output quickly, making supply more elastic.

lesson: Price elasticity of supply measures how much quantity supplied responds to a price change. The logic differs from demand: it is about whether producers CAN react, not whether they want to.

Time dominates everything. Given an hour, a farmer cannot grow more wheat at any price, so supply is almost perfectly inelastic. Given a season, they can plant more. Given a decade, they can buy land. Spare capacity works the same way: a factory running at half capacity can expand output quickly; one already at full stretch cannot.

Whether stock can be stored matters too, as does how easily workers and machines can be moved between uses. This is why primary commodities tend to have low PES and manufactured goods higher — and why commodity prices swing so violently when demand moves.

topics.title: Role of government in microeconomics
essentials: Indirect taxes (specific and ad valorem): effect on price, quantity, consumer and producer surplus, government revenue, and welfare loss.
Subsidies: effect on price, quantity, government cost, and welfare.
Price ceilings (maximum prices) set below equilibrium: shortages, rationing, parallel markets, and welfare loss.
Price floors (minimum prices) set above equilibrium: surpluses, government buying, and welfare loss.
Minimum wage as a price floor in the labour market.
Tax incidence: the burden splits according to the relative elasticities of demand and supply.
diagrams: Specific and ad valorem indirect taxes
Price ceiling with shortage and welfare loss
Price floor with surplus and welfare loss
hl: Calculating from a diagram: tax revenue, subsidy cost, consumer and producer expenditure, and welfare loss
topics.trap: A price ceiling only binds if it is set BELOW equilibrium, and a price floor only if ABOVE. A non-binding control changes nothing — examiners set this deliberately.

terms.definition: A legally imposed maximum price, which causes a shortage when set below equilibrium.
A legally imposed minimum price, which causes a surplus when set above equilibrium.
An indirect tax of a fixed amount per unit, shifting supply upward in parallel.
An indirect tax charged as a percentage of price, so the supply curve pivots rather than shifting in parallel.
The division of the burden of an indirect tax between consumers and producers, determined by relative elasticities.
The loss of community surplus that occurs when output is not at the allocatively efficient level.

lesson: Governments intervene in markets for two broad reasons: to change what gets produced, and to change who can afford it. The tools are taxes, subsidies and price controls, and each has a diagram you must be able to draw and explain.

An indirect tax shifts supply up by the tax per unit. Price rises, quantity falls, and the gap between what consumers pay and what producers keep is the tax. Who actually bears it is decided by elasticity, not by who writes the cheque: the side less able to respond absorbs more. Tax fuel, whose demand is inelastic, and consumers pay most of it. A subsidy works in reverse, shifting supply down, lowering the price paid and raising the price received, with the difference costing the government.

Price controls are blunter. A maximum price below equilibrium protects consumers but creates a shortage — and shortages get rationed somehow, often by queues or parallel markets. A minimum price above equilibrium protects producers but creates a surplus someone must buy or destroy. Both only bite if set on the correct side of equilibrium; a maximum price above equilibrium changes nothing at all, and examiners set that deliberately.

topics.title: Market failure — externalities and common pool resources
essentials: Externalities as costs or benefits falling on third parties, so private and social costs or benefits diverge.
The four cases: negative production, positive production, negative consumption, positive consumption externalities.
Marginal private cost/benefit versus marginal social cost/benefit, and the welfare loss triangle.
Common pool resources: rivalrous but non-excludable, leading to over-use — the tragedy of the commons.
Policy responses: indirect taxes, carbon taxes, tradable permits, legislation and regulation, education, subsidies, direct provision, collective self-governance.
Sustainability and the need for international cooperation, and why enforcement is hard.
diagrams: Negative production externality with welfare loss
Positive consumption externality with welfare loss
hl: Calculating welfare loss from a diagram
topics.trap: Draw the welfare loss triangle and shade it. Many answers describe the externality perfectly and never show the loss, which caps criterion A and the diagram dimension of the markband.

terms.definition: A cost or benefit falling on a third party not involved in the transaction, causing private and social costs or benefits to diverge.
The cost to the producer of supplying one more unit.
The total cost to society of one more unit, including any external costs.
A resource that is rivalrous but non-excludable, and therefore prone to over-use.
The depletion of a common pool resource because each user gains the full benefit of use while bearing only part of the cost.
A tax per unit of carbon emitted, intended to internalise the external cost of pollution.
A saleable licence to emit a fixed quantity of pollutant, capping total emissions while letting the market allocate them.

lesson: Sometimes a market clears perfectly and still gets the answer wrong, because the price does not include every cost. A factory that pollutes a river pays for its labour and materials but not for the fishing it destroys downstream. That uncounted cost falls on a third party, and it is called an externality.

Draw it as two cost curves. Marginal private cost is what the firm pays. Marginal social cost includes the damage as well, so it sits above. The market produces where private cost meets demand, which is beyond the socially optimal quantity — so society gets too much of the good and too much pollution. The triangle between the two quantities is the welfare loss, and you must shade it. Most answers describe the externality perfectly and never draw the loss, which caps the diagram mark.

Common pool resources fail the same way. A fish stock is rivalrous but nobody can be excluded, so each boat takes the full benefit of one more catch while the cost of depletion is shared by all. Everyone acting sensibly destroys the thing everyone depends on. The policy responses — taxes, tradable permits, regulation, education, collective self-governance — all try to make the private decision reflect the social one.

topics.title: Market failure — public goods
essentials: Public goods are non-rivalrous and non-excludable.
The free rider problem means the private market will under-provide or not provide them at all.
Government responses: direct provision funded by taxation, or contracting out to the private sector.
topics.trap: 'Public good' does not mean 'good provided by the government'. Test both properties. Healthcare and education are usually merit goods, not public goods.

terms.definition: A good that is both non-rivalrous and non-excludable, and therefore under-provided or not provided by the free market.
Consumption by one person does not reduce the amount available to others.
It is not possible to prevent people who have not paid from consuming the good.
The tendency for people to consume a non-excludable good without paying, so the market fails to supply it.

lesson: A public good is defined by two properties, and you must test both. Non-rivalrous: one person consuming it does not reduce what is left for anyone else. Non-excludable: you cannot stop people who have not paid from benefiting.

A lighthouse is the classic case. Its beam is not used up by the ship that sees it, and no ship can be prevented from seeing it. Now consider running one as a business: every captain benefits whether or not they pay, so the rational move is to wait for someone else to pay. That is the free rider problem, and it means the private market provides too little or nothing at all.

Be careful with the label. A public good is not simply a good the government provides. Healthcare and education are usually rivalrous and excludable — they are merit goods, under-consumed rather than un-providable. Getting this wrong turns a definition question into a lost mark.

topics.title: Market failure — asymmetric information
essentials: Asymmetric information exists where one party to a transaction knows more than the other.
Adverse selection occurs before the transaction — the used car and insurance markets are the standard cases.
Moral hazard occurs after it, once behaviour changes because someone else bears the risk.
Government responses: legislation, regulation, provision of information.
Private responses: signalling by the informed party and screening by the uninformed.
hl: Entire topic is HL only
topics.trap: Adverse selection is before the deal, moral hazard after. Getting them the wrong way round is the most common HL slip here.

terms.definition: A situation where one party to a transaction has more or better information than the other.
A market failure occurring before a transaction, where the better-informed party self-selects to the detriment of the other.
A market failure occurring after a transaction, where one party changes behaviour because another bears the risk.
Action by the informed party to credibly convey information to the uninformed party.
Action by the uninformed party to draw information out of the informed party.

lesson: Markets assume both sides know what they are trading. Often one side knows far more, and that asymmetry breaks the market in two distinct ways you must not confuse.

Adverse selection happens BEFORE the transaction. A seller of a used car knows whether it is a lemon; the buyer does not, so offers only an average price. Owners of good cars refuse that price and withdraw, leaving worse cars, so buyers offer less still. Quality spirals down. The same logic explains why insurers fear that only the sickest people want health cover.
Moral hazard happens AFTER. Once insured, a driver takes more risks, because someone else now bears the cost. Nothing was hidden at signing; behaviour changed afterwards.

Both have responses. The informed party can signal — a warranty, a qualification — and the uninformed can screen, offering deals that sort people by their own choices. Governments legislate for disclosure and provide information directly.

topics.title: Market failure — market power
essentials: Costs: fixed and variable, total and average, and marginal cost; the short run versus the long run.
Diminishing marginal returns in the short run; economies and diseconomies of scale in the long run.
Revenue: total, average and marginal, and how they differ under price-taking and price-making.
Profit maximisation at MC = MR; normal and abnormal profit; the shut-down and break-even rules.
Perfect competition: many firms, homogeneous products, free entry, price takers; allocative and productive efficiency in the long run.
Monopoly: barriers to entry, price making, abnormal profit sustained in the long run, welfare loss; natural monopoly.
Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, some price-setting power, no long-run abnormal profit.
Oligopoly: few firms, interdependence, collusion and cartels, game theory and the prisoner's dilemma, non-price competition.
Policy responses to market power: regulation, legislation, nationalisation, trade liberalisation.
diagrams: Perfect competition: firm and industry, short run and long run
Monopolistic competition, short run and long run
hl: Entire topic is HL only
Calculating costs, revenues and profit from data
topics.trap: MC cuts AC and AVC at their minimum points, always. Drawing it otherwise loses marks before the argument is read.

terms.definition: The ability of a firm to influence the price of its product rather than take it as given.
A market with many small firms selling a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, and perfect information, in which firms are price takers.
A market with a single seller protected by barriers to entry, able to set price.
An industry in which economies of scale are so large that one firm can supply the whole market at lower average cost than several.
A market with many firms selling differentiated products with low barriers to entry, giving each limited price-setting power.
A market dominated by a few interdependent firms, where each firm's decisions depend on rivals' expected responses.
An agreement between firms to restrict output or fix prices in order to raise joint profits.
Profit above normal profit, earned when total revenue exceeds total cost including opportunity cost.
Producing at the lowest point of the average cost curve, so no output is wasted.

lesson: Market power is the ability to set price rather than accept it, and everything in this topic follows from that one difference.

A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: many rivals, an identical product, free entry. It can sell all it wants at the market price, so average revenue equals marginal revenue and the demand curve it faces is horizontal. In the long run, free entry competes away abnormal profit and the firm ends up producing at lowest average cost — productively and allocatively efficient.

A monopolist faces the whole market demand curve, which slopes down. To sell one more unit it must cut price on every unit, so marginal revenue falls faster than price and lies below it — twice as steep, meeting the horizontal axis halfway along. It produces where marginal cost equals marginal revenue and charges what demand will bear, which means output is lower and price higher than under competition. The gap is welfare loss.

Between the two sit monopolistic competition, where differentiation gives limited pricing power that entry erodes, and oligopoly, where a few large firms are interdependent and each one's best move depends on what rivals do — which is why collusion is tempting and cartels are unstable.

topics.title: The market's inability to achieve equity
essentials: Markets allocate on ability to pay, which need not produce a fair distribution.
Merit goods are under-consumed and demerit goods over-consumed relative to what is socially desirable.
The efficiency versus equity trade-off in policy design.
Government responses and their costs, including the incentive effects of redistribution.
hl: Entire topic is HL only
topics.trap: Equity is normative. Say whose conception of fairness you are applying — that acknowledgement is exactly what the top evaluation band rewards.

terms.definition: A good that is under-consumed relative to what is socially desirable, because consumers undervalue its private benefits.
A good that is over-consumed relative to what is socially desirable, because consumers undervalue its private costs.
Fairness in the distribution of income, wealth or opportunity — a normative concept, distinct from equality.

lesson: Markets allocate by ability to pay. That is efficient in a specific technical sense and says nothing at all about whether the outcome is fair. Someone with no income exerts no demand, however urgent their need.

So markets under-provide merit goods, whose private benefits people undervalue — vaccination, education, insurance — and over-provide demerit goods whose private costs they undervalue. The market is not making an arithmetic error; it is answering a different question from the one society is asking.

Correcting this means accepting a trade-off. Redistribution through progressive taxes and transfers reduces inequality but can blunt incentives to work and invest. That tension between equity and efficiency is the substance of the topic, and the top-band answers are the ones that name whose idea of fairness they are applying — because equity is normative, and saying so is the evaluation.

topics.title: Measuring economic activity and illustrating its variations
essentials: The circular flow of income, including injections (investment, government spending, exports) and leakages (saving, taxation, imports).
GDP measured three ways — output, income, expenditure — and why they are equal.
GDP versus GNI, and nominal versus real; why real figures are needed for comparison over time.
GDP per capita, and purchasing power parity for comparison across countries.
Limitations of national income statistics: the informal economy, unpaid work, externalities, distribution, and quality of life.
Alternative measures: the OECD Better Life Index, the Happy Planet Index, and the concept of green GDP.
The business cycle: expansion, peak, contraction, trough, and the long-term growth trend.
diagrams: Business cycle showing the trend line
hl: Calculating nominal and real GDP and GNI from data
Calculating GDP using a price deflator
topics.trap: Real GDP per capita is the figure that speaks to living standards. Quoting total nominal GDP growth in a development answer is a weak argument that examiners routinely penalise.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period.
GDP plus net income from abroad, measuring income earned by a country's residents wherever it is generated.
GDP measured at current prices, so it rises with both output and inflation.
GDP adjusted for changes in the price level, so it reflects changes in output alone.
An exchange rate adjustment that equalises the cost of a common basket of goods, allowing fairer comparison of income between countries.
The short-run fluctuation of real GDP around its long-term growth trend, through expansion, peak, contraction and trough.

lesson: Macroeconomics needs a number for the size of an economy, and that number is GDP: the market value of everything final produced inside a country in a period. Final matters — count the bread and the flour and you have counted the flour twice.

It can be measured three ways that must give the same answer: what was produced, what was earned making it, and what was spent buying it. Output equals income equals expenditure. That identity is why the circular flow diagram works: money leaves households as spending and returns as wages, with injections from investment, government and exports, and leakages into saving, tax and imports.

Two corrections turn GDP into something meaningful. Adjust for prices to get REAL GDP, or growth is just inflation in disguise. Divide by population to get GDP per capita, or a big poor country looks rich. For comparisons across countries add purchasing power parity, since the same money buys different amounts in different places.
Even then it is a poor measure of welfare. It ignores unpaid work, the informal economy, environmental damage and the distribution of income entirely. A country can grow while most people get poorer.

topics.title: Variations in economic activity — aggregate demand and aggregate supply
essentials: AD = C + I + G + (X − M), and the determinants of each component.
Why the AD curve slopes down: wealth, interest rate and international trade effects.
Short-run aggregate supply and its determinants (costs of production, indirect taxes, subsidies).
Two models of long-run supply: the monetarist/new classical vertical LRAS at full employment, and the Keynesian AS curve with its horizontal, upward-sloping and vertical sections.
Equilibrium: inflationary and deflationary (recessionary) gaps.
The multiplier effect and how a change in an injection produces a larger change in national income.
hl: Calculating the multiplier from MPC, MPS, MPT and MPM
Using the multiplier to find the change in real GDP
topics.trap: Choose your AS model deliberately and say why. The Keynesian and new classical models give different answers about whether the economy self-corrects — that choice IS the evaluation.

terms.definition: The total planned spending on domestic output at each price level: consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports.
The total output firms are willing to supply at each price level when the prices of factors of production are fixed.
The level of output an economy can sustain when all resources are fully employed, independent of the price level in the monetarist model.
The shortfall of real output below the full employment level, caused by insufficient aggregate demand.
The excess of real output above the full employment level, generating upward pressure on the price level.
The factor by which an initial change in injections changes national income, determined by the marginal propensity to withdraw.

lesson: Aggregate demand is total planned spending on domestic output: consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports. Investment here means firms buying physical capital — machinery, buildings — not someone buying shares, which just changes who owns what.

Aggregate supply is what producers will supply at each price level, and here economists genuinely disagree. The monetarist view draws long-run supply as vertical at full employment: in the long run output is set by resources and technology, so demand only moves prices. The Keynesian view draws it flat when there is spare capacity, sloping as the economy tightens, and vertical only at full employment.

That disagreement is the whole evaluation. On the flat Keynesian section, extra demand raises output with almost no inflation, so stimulus works. On a vertical curve, the same stimulus only raises prices. Say which model you are using and how the answer changes under the other, and you are writing top-band evaluation rather than describing a diagram.

One more mechanism: the multiplier. An injection is spent, becomes someone's income, and is partly spent again. How far it circulates depends on how much leaks into saving, tax and imports at each round.

topics.title: Macroeconomic objectives
essentials: Low unemployment: measurement by the unemployment rate, and its limitations (hidden unemployment, underemployment, participation).
Types of unemployment: structural, frictional, seasonal, and cyclical (demand-deficient), with their different causes and cures.
Costs of unemployment, economic and social.
Low and stable inflation: measurement by CPI and its limitations.
Demand-pull and cost-push inflation; the costs of inflation and of deflation; disinflation.
Economic growth: actual versus potential, shown on a PPC or AD/AS diagram.
Conflicts between objectives, including the short-run Phillips curve trade-off between unemployment and inflation.
diagrams: Actual and potential growth on a PPC and on AD/AS
hl: Constructing a weighted price index and calculating inflation from it
Calculating the unemployment rate
topics.trap: Deflation and disinflation are not the same. Deflation is a falling price level; disinflation is a falling rate of inflation with prices still rising.

terms.definition: The number of people unemployed expressed as a percentage of the labour force.
Unemployment caused by a mismatch between workers' skills or location and the jobs available.
Short-term unemployment while people move between jobs.
Unemployment caused by a fall in aggregate demand during a downturn, also called demand-deficient unemployment.
A sustained increase in the general price level over time.
A sustained decrease in the general price level over time.
A fall in the rate of inflation, where prices are still rising but more slowly.
A weighted index measuring the change in price of a representative basket of goods bought by a typical household.
Inflation caused by rising aggregate demand outstripping the economy's capacity to supply.
Inflation caused by rising costs of production shifting short-run aggregate supply leftward.
A curve showing the short-run inverse relationship between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment.

lesson: Governments chase four things at once: low unemployment, low and stable inflation, economic growth, and a sustainable external position. The interesting part is that these conflict.

Unemployment comes in kinds that need different cures. Frictional is people between jobs and is fairly harmless. Structural is a mismatch — skills or location no longer match the jobs available — and is the hardest to fix, because retraining takes years. Cyclical is caused by a fall in aggregate demand and is the one demand-side policy can actually reach.

Inflation also comes in two flavours, and the distinction decides the policy. Demand-pull is too much spending against limited capacity: cool demand and it eases. Cost-push is rising production costs shifting supply left, which raises prices AND cuts output at the same time. Raising interest rates against cost-push inflation works only by crushing demand further — which is why it is such a reliable evaluation point.
Keep deflation and disinflation apart. Deflation is prices falling. Disinflation is prices still rising, just more slowly. Confusing them reverses your argument.

topics.title: Economics of inequality and poverty
essentials: Inequality of income and of wealth, and why the two differ.
The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient as measures.
Absolute versus relative poverty, and the difficulty of drawing a poverty line.
Causes of inequality and poverty: inheritance, discrimination, unequal education and health, unequal status and power.
Consequences: lower living standards, lower growth, reduced social cohesion.
Redistribution policies: progressive taxation, transfer payments, provision of merit goods, and universal basic income.
The equity versus efficiency trade-off in redistribution.
diagrams: Lorenz curve and the line of equality
Progressive, proportional and regressive tax structures
hl: Calculating the Gini coefficient conceptually from a Lorenz curve
Calculating marginal and average tax rates from a tax schedule
topics.trap: A higher Gini coefficient means MORE inequality. The Lorenz curve bows further from the 45-degree line. Reversing this reverses your whole argument.

terms.definition: A curve plotting the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of population, showing the degree of income inequality.
A number between 0 and 1 summarising income inequality, where 0 is perfect equality and higher values mean greater inequality.
A condition where income is insufficient to meet basic needs such as food, shelter and clothing.
A condition where income is substantially below the average for the society in question.
A tax that takes a rising proportion of income as income rises.
A tax that takes a falling proportion of income as income rises.
A payment from government to individuals for which no good or service is exchanged, such as a pension or benefit.

lesson: Income inequality is not the same as poverty, and neither is the same as unfairness. Inequality is about the spread; poverty is about the floor.

The Lorenz curve plots the cumulative share of income against the cumulative share of population. Perfect equality is the 45-degree line, where the poorest 20% earn 20% of income. Real economies bow below it, and the further the bow, the greater the inequality. The Gini coefficient turns that gap into one number between 0 and 1 — and remember, HIGHER means MORE unequal.

Poverty splits into absolute, where income cannot meet basic needs, and relative, where income is far below the norm for that society. Both depend on where you draw the line, which is why moving the line changes the count without changing anyone's life.

Redistribution uses progressive taxes, transfer payments and provision of merit goods. Each reduces inequality and each has a cost — in incentives, in administration, or in the taxes needed to fund it. Naming the cost is what separates description from evaluation.

topics.title: Demand management — monetary policy
essentials: The central bank's goals and its independence.
The interest rate as the main tool, and how it is set to influence AD.
The transmission mechanism: interest rates affect consumption, investment, the exchange rate and hence net exports.
Expansionary policy in a recession, contractionary policy against inflation.
Strengths: incremental, reversible, free of political pressure, quick to implement.
Limitations: time lags, the liquidity trap and the zero lower bound, low confidence blunting the effect, conflict with other objectives.
diagrams: Money market showing the interest rate
hl: The money market: demand for and supply of money
Quantitative easing as a tool when rates hit the lower bound
topics.trap: Monetary policy cannot fix cost-push inflation without cutting output. Saying so is one of the most reliable evaluation points in Unit 3.

terms.definition: Central bank action on interest rates and the money supply to influence aggregate demand.
The price of borrowing money, or the reward for saving, expressed as a percentage.
Lowering interest rates to raise consumption and investment and so increase aggregate demand.
Raising interest rates to reduce aggregate demand and ease inflationary pressure.
A situation where interest rates are so low that further cuts fail to stimulate borrowing and spending.
Central bank purchase of financial assets to increase the money supply when interest rates are already near zero.

lesson: Monetary policy is the central bank changing the price of borrowing to steer aggregate demand. The tool is the interest rate; the target is usually an inflation figure.

Follow the transmission. Cut rates and borrowing is cheaper, so households buy more on credit and firms find more investment projects worth doing. Saving becomes less attractive, so more income is spent. The currency tends to weaken as capital seeks better returns elsewhere, which helps exports. All four routes raise aggregate demand.

Its strengths are practical: it can be adjusted in small steps, reversed quickly, and set by an independent bank insulated from elections. Its weaknesses are equally practical. It works with long and variable lags. In a deep recession rates hit the zero lower bound and cannot fall further, which is when quantitative easing appears and when fiscal policy becomes the stronger tool. And confidence can defeat it entirely: if firms expect no customers, no interest rate makes a new factory worth building.

topics.title: Demand management — fiscal policy
essentials: Government revenue and expenditure; the budget outcome as deficit, surplus or balance; government (national) debt.
Expansionary and contractionary fiscal policy and their effect on AD.
Automatic stabilisers: progressive taxes and unemployment benefits damping the cycle without new decisions.
The multiplier magnifying any fiscal change.
Strengths: targeted, effective in deep recession, can build potential capacity through infrastructure.
Limitations: political constraints, time lags, crowding out, debt sustainability.
diagrams: Expansionary fiscal policy closing a deflationary gap
Contractionary fiscal policy closing an inflationary gap
hl: Calculating the multiplier and the resulting change in real GDP
Using the multiplier to size a fiscal intervention
topics.trap: A budget deficit is a yearly flow; national debt is the accumulated stock. A government can cut its deficit while its debt still rises.

terms.definition: Government use of taxation and spending to influence aggregate demand.
The amount by which government spending exceeds government revenue in a given year.
The accumulated stock of past budget deficits still outstanding.
A feature of the tax and benefit system that dampens the business cycle without new government decisions.
The reduction in private investment caused by government borrowing raising interest rates.

lesson: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxation used to influence aggregate demand. Spend more or tax less and demand rises; the reverse cools it.

Some of this happens without any decision at all. In a downturn, incomes fall so tax receipts fall, and unemployment benefits rise automatically. These automatic stabilisers damp the cycle before any politician acts.

Deliberate fiscal policy has a real advantage over monetary policy: it can be targeted at the regions or groups that need it, and infrastructure spending raises long-run capacity as well as current demand. It also has real limits. It is politically hard to reverse, because cutting spending loses votes. It works with lags — recognising the problem, deciding, and implementing all take time. Government borrowing may crowd out private investment by pushing up interest rates.

Keep the flow and the stock straight. The deficit is this year's shortfall; the debt is the accumulated total. A government can cut its deficit while its debt still rises, and confusing the two is a common and costly slip.

topics.title: Supply-side policies
essentials: The aim: to increase potential output by shifting LRAS or the Keynesian AS right.
Market-based policies: labour market reform, deregulation, privatisation, trade liberalisation, incentive-related tax cuts.
Interventionist policies: investment in education and training, healthcare, infrastructure, research and development, and industrial policy.
Effects on growth, unemployment, inflation and the trade balance — potentially improving several objectives at once.
Limitations: long time lags, high cost, equity concerns from market-based reforms, uncertain outcomes.
diagrams: Supply-side policy on the Keynesian AS curve
topics.trap: Supply-side policies are the only ones that can lower inflation and unemployment together. That makes them a strong closing evaluation in almost any macro policy question.

terms.definition: Policy aimed at increasing the productive capacity of the economy by shifting long-run aggregate supply rightward.
Policy that increases capacity by reducing government interference, such as deregulation, privatisation and lower marginal tax rates.
Policy that increases capacity through direct government investment in education, healthcare, infrastructure or research.
The stock of skills, knowledge and health embodied in the workforce that raises productivity.

lesson: Demand-side policies move aggregate demand along the supply curve. Supply-side policies try to move the supply curve itself — to raise what the economy is capable of producing.

The market-based version works by sharpening incentives and removing obstacles: deregulation, privatisation, labour market reform, lower marginal tax rates, trade liberalisation. The interventionist version works by building capacity directly: education and training, healthcare, infrastructure, research and development.

The attraction is that supply-side policy can improve several objectives at once. Shift long-run supply right and you get more output, lower unemployment AND lower prices — something no demand-side policy can do, since raising demand raises prices too.

The catch is time and cost. Educating a workforce takes a decade and the benefits are hard to measure. Market-based reforms often raise inequality even where they raise efficiency. Saying that supply-side policy is the only lever that improves inflation and unemployment together, then naming the lag and the equity cost, is a complete evaluation in two sentences.

topics.title: Benefits of international trade
essentials: Gains from trade: lower prices, greater choice, economies of scale, more competition, access to resources, faster growth.
Absolute and comparative advantage, and specialisation according to lower opportunity cost.
Limitations of the comparative advantage model: transport costs, assumed constant costs, factor immobility, ignoring externalities.
diagrams: Production possibilities curves illustrating comparative advantage
hl: Calculating opportunity costs from output or input data to identify comparative advantage
Deriving the terms of trade at which both parties gain
topics.trap: Comparative advantage rests on opportunity cost, not on who produces more. A country can hold absolute advantage in everything and still gain from trade.

terms.definition: The ability of a country to produce more of a good than another using the same resources.
The ability of a country to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country.
The ratio of an index of export prices to an index of import prices, multiplied by one hundred.
Concentrating production on the goods in which a country has a comparative advantage.

lesson: Countries trade for the same reason people do: they are better at different things. The surprising part is that trade still pays even when one country is better at everything.

Absolute advantage means producing more with the same resources. Comparative advantage means producing at a lower OPPORTUNITY COST, and it is comparative advantage that drives trade. A surgeon may type faster than their secretary, but every hour typing costs an hour of surgery, so both gain when each specialises. Countries work the same way.

So specialise where opportunity cost is lowest, trade, and both parties consume beyond what they could produce alone. The gains show up as lower prices, more choice, larger scale, sharper competition and access to resources you do not have.

The model is a simplification and saying how is legitimate evaluation. It assumes costs stay constant, ignores transport, assumes factors can move between industries at home, and takes no account of environmental damage or who inside a country actually gains.

topics.title: Types of trade protection
essentials: Tariffs: effect on price, domestic production, consumption, imports, government revenue, and welfare.
Quotas: quantitative limits, with the gain going to importers rather than the government.
Subsidies to domestic producers as protection.
Administrative barriers: standards, licensing, customs procedures.
In every case: identify winners (domestic producers, sometimes government) and losers (consumers, foreign producers, overall welfare).
diagrams: Tariff with government revenue and welfare loss
Quota with the quota rent identified
hl: Calculating from a tariff diagram: revenue, welfare loss, changes in domestic production, consumption and imports
Calculating the effects of a quota and of a subsidy
topics.trap: On a tariff diagram there are TWO welfare loss triangles — production inefficiency and consumption inefficiency. Shading only one loses the calculation mark.

terms.definition: A tax on imported goods, raising their price and reducing the quantity imported.
A physical limit on the quantity of a good that may be imported in a given period.
A payment to domestic producers that lowers their costs and lets them undercut imports.
A non-tariff obstacle to trade such as a standard, licence or customs procedure that raises the cost of importing.
The extra revenue captured by importers who hold the right to sell within a quota at the raised domestic price.

lesson: Protection means making imports less competitive, and the tools differ in who captures the benefit.

A tariff is a tax on imports. Domestic price rises, domestic producers expand, consumers buy less, imports shrink and the government collects revenue on what still comes in. On the diagram there are TWO welfare loss triangles — production inefficiency where high-cost domestic output replaces cheaper imports, and consumption inefficiency where buyers priced out lose surplus. Shading only one loses the calculation mark.

A quota caps quantity instead of raising price directly. The price effect is similar, but the extra revenue goes to whoever holds the right to import rather than to the government. That quota rent is the key evaluative difference from a tariff.

Subsidies to domestic producers lower their costs so they can undercut imports without any visible price rise, which makes them politically attractive and fiscally expensive. Administrative barriers — standards, licensing, slow customs — do the same job while being harder to challenge as protectionism.

topics.title: Arguments for and against trade control/protection
essentials: Arguments for: infant industry, national security, health and safety standards, environmental standards, anti-dumping, protecting employment, correcting a current account deficit, government revenue.
Arguments against: higher prices and less choice, loss of the gains from comparative advantage, protected inefficiency, retaliation and trade wars, damage to exporters.
Weighing them depends on time horizon, the industry, and the alternatives available.
topics.trap: The infant industry argument requires a credible exit. Protection with no timetable for removal becomes permanent inefficiency — say this and you have your evaluation.

terms.definition: The case for protecting a new domestic industry until it achieves the economies of scale needed to compete internationally.
Selling exports below cost of production, or below the price charged at home, in order to capture a foreign market.
An escalating exchange of protectionist measures between countries in retaliation for each other's barriers.

lesson: Every argument for protection is an argument about something other than efficiency, which is why they are worth taking seriously and worth testing.

The infant industry case says a new industry needs shelter until it reaches the scale to compete. It is theoretically sound and practically dangerous: protection with no timetable becomes permanent inefficiency, and the industry lobbies to keep it. National security, health and safety standards, environmental standards and anti-dumping measures are similarly legitimate in principle and routinely abused as disguised protection.

Protecting employment is the most emotionally powerful and economically weakest: it saves visible jobs in the protected industry at the cost of diffuse losses everywhere else, including in exporters hit by retaliation.

Against all of it: higher prices, less choice, protected inefficiency, and the risk of a trade war in which everyone ends up worse off than before. The strongest answers do not pick a side in the abstract — they say what the answer depends on.

topics.title: Economic integration
essentials: Preferential trade agreements, bilateral and regional.
Stages of integration: free trade area, customs union, common market, monetary union, full economic union.
Trade creation and trade diversion.
Advantages and disadvantages of monetary union, including the loss of independent monetary policy and exchange rate adjustment.
The World Trade Organization: role, and the limits of its power.
topics.trap: A customs union adds a common external tariff to a free trade area. Getting the ladder of stages in order is a straightforward mark you should never drop.

terms.definition: An agreement in which members remove trade barriers between themselves but keep their own external tariffs.
A free trade area whose members also adopt a common external tariff against non-members.
A customs union that additionally allows free movement of factors of production between members.
A common market whose members share a single currency and a single monetary policy.
The replacement of higher-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from a member of a trading bloc.
The replacement of lower-cost imports from a non-member with higher-cost imports from a member of a trading bloc.

lesson: Economic integration is countries agreeing to treat each other differently from everyone else, and it comes in a ladder you should be able to recite in order.

A free trade area removes barriers between members but each keeps its own external tariffs. A customs union adds a common external tariff. A common market adds free movement of factors — labour and capital. A monetary union adds a shared currency and therefore a single monetary policy. Full economic union adds harmonised fiscal policy.

The economics is not automatically positive. Trade creation is good: high-cost domestic production is replaced by cheaper production from a member. Trade diversion is not: cheaper production from a non-member is replaced by more expensive production from a member, purely because of the tariff wall.

Monetary union carries the sharpest trade-off. Members gain price transparency and lose exchange rate risk, but give up the ability to set interest rates or devalue in response to a shock that hits them and not their partners.

topics.title: Exchange rates
essentials: Floating rates determined by demand for and supply of a currency; appreciation and depreciation.
Determinants: trade flows, investment flows, interest rate differentials, speculation, relative inflation.
Fixed and managed exchange rate systems; devaluation and revaluation.
Effects of a change in the exchange rate on inflation, employment, growth and the current account.
Central bank intervention to influence the rate, and its limits.
diagrams: Foreign exchange market: appreciation and depreciation
Central bank intervention to maintain a fixed rate
hl: Calculating exchange rates and converting values between currencies
topics.trap: Label the axes 'price of currency A in terms of currency B' and 'quantity of currency A'. Unlabelled forex axes are the fastest way to lose the diagram marks in Unit 4.

terms.definition: The price of one currency expressed in terms of another.
A rise in the value of a currency against another under a floating exchange rate system.
A fall in the value of a currency against another under a floating exchange rate system.
A deliberate reduction in the value of a currency by the authorities under a fixed exchange rate system.
A system in which the rate floats but the central bank intervenes to limit its movement.

lesson: An exchange rate is just the price of one currency in another, set — under a float — by supply and demand in the foreign exchange market.

Demand for a currency comes from foreigners buying its exports, investing in its assets, or speculating that it will rise. Supply comes from residents doing the same abroad. So higher interest rates tend to attract capital and push the currency up; higher relative inflation pushes it down.

A rise is an appreciation, a fall a depreciation. Under a fixed system the equivalent deliberate moves are revaluation and devaluation. The effects run in opposite directions and both are examinable: a depreciation makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home, helping the trade balance and employment but importing inflation. An appreciation does the reverse — it helps hold inflation down and hurts exporters.

When you draw the market, label the axes properly: price of currency A in terms of currency B, and quantity of currency A. Unlabelled forex axes are the quickest way to lose the diagram marks in this unit.

topics.title: Balance of payments
essentials: Structure: the current account, the capital account, and the financial account.
Components of the current account: trade in goods, trade in services, primary income, secondary income.
Why the accounts must balance overall, so a current account deficit is matched by a financial account surplus.
Consequences of a persistent current account deficit and of a surplus.
Correcting a deficit: expenditure switching, expenditure reducing, and supply-side measures.
The Marshall-Lerner condition and the J-curve effect.
hl: Calculating the balance on the current account and its components from data
Applying the Marshall-Lerner condition
topics.trap: The Marshall-Lerner condition is that the sum of PED for exports and imports exceeds 1. Only then does depreciation improve the current account — which is exactly why the J-curve dips first.

terms.definition: A record of all transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world over a period.
The part of the balance of payments recording trade in goods and services, primary income and secondary income.
The part of the balance of payments recording transactions in financial assets, including direct and portfolio investment.
A situation in which the outflows recorded on the current account exceed the inflows.
The condition that a depreciation improves the current account only if the sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds one.
The pattern by which a depreciation worsens the current account before improving it, as elasticities rise over time.

lesson: The balance of payments records every transaction between a country's residents and the rest of the world, and it always balances. That is not an economic result; it is bookkeeping. Money that leaves one account arrives in another.

The current account covers trade in goods and services, primary income such as profits and wages from abroad, and secondary income such as remittances and aid. The financial account covers transactions in assets — direct investment, portfolio flows, reserves. A current account deficit is therefore matched by a financial account surplus: a country buying more than it sells is financing the gap by borrowing or selling assets.
Whether a persistent deficit matters depends on what the borrowing bought. Financing productive investment is very different from financing consumption.

Correcting one uses expenditure switching — a depreciation, or protection — or expenditure reducing, meaning cutting demand overall. Depreciation only works if the Marshall-Lerner condition holds: the elasticities of demand for exports and imports must sum to more than one. In the short run they rarely do, which is why the current account often worsens before it improves. That is the J-curve.

topics.title: Sustainable development
essentials: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations' ability to meet theirs.
The tension between economic growth and environmental sustainability.
Poverty as both cause and consequence of environmental degradation.
The Sustainable Development Goals as a framework and a measurement problem.
hl: Sustainability constraints on long-run growth
topics.trap: Sustainable development is broader than environmental protection — it includes economic and social sustainability. Treating it as only 'green' narrows your answer.

terms.definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
The set of global objectives adopted by the United Nations covering poverty, health, education, equality and the environment.

lesson: Sustainable development means meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs. The definition is worth learning exactly, because the marks are in the intergenerational clause.

The tension is real. Growth uses resources and produces waste, and a lot of what counts as income today is drawn from natural capital that will not be there tomorrow. GDP treats cutting down a forest as production and records no loss when the forest is gone.

Poverty makes this harder, not easier. People with no margin cannot prioritise the long run: they farm marginal land and burn what they can find, degrading the resources they depend on. Environmental sustainability and development are therefore entangled rather than opposed.

Sustainability is broader than the environment: it also means economic sustainability, not building growth on unsustainable debt, and social sustainability. Treating the topic as purely green narrows your answer.

topics.title: Measuring development
essentials: Economic growth versus economic development: growth is a rise in output, development is a broader rise in well-being and freedom.
Single indicators: GDP and GNI per capita at PPP, health indicators, education indicators, energy and environment indicators.
Composite indicators: the Human Development Index and its three dimensions; the inequality-adjusted HDI; the Gender Inequality Index.
Strengths and limitations of every indicator, particularly averaging away distribution.
topics.trap: HDI combines income, health and education. A country can post strong GDP growth and a flat HDI — that gap is usually the most interesting thing to say.

terms.definition: An increase in real output, usually measured as the percentage change in real GDP.
A broad improvement in living standards, including health, education, income and freedom of choice.
A composite index combining life expectancy, education and gross national income per capita at purchasing power parity.
A measure that combines several separate indicators into a single number.

lesson: Growth and development are different claims. Growth is more output — a bigger real GDP. Development is a broader improvement in how people live: health, education, security, and the freedom to make choices.

They usually move together and sometimes do not, which is exactly what makes the comparison interesting. A country can grow fast on oil revenue while life expectancy and schooling stand still, if the income reaches few people.

Single indicators each capture one dimension: GNI per capita at PPP for income, life expectancy for health, mean and expected years of schooling for education. Composite indicators combine them, and the Human Development Index is the one to know — income, health and education in a single figure between 0 and 1.

Every measure hides something. HDI averages away distribution, which is why the inequality-adjusted HDI exists. The Gender Inequality Index captures what the others miss entirely. The strongest answers name what a chosen indicator cannot see.

topics.title: Barriers to economic growth and/or economic development
essentials: Poverty traps and low-income cycles of low saving, low investment and low productivity.

Economic barriers: rising economic inequality, lack of access to infrastructure and appropriate technology, low levels of human capital, dependence on primary exports, volatile commodity prices, adverse terms of trade, capital flight, indebtedness.
Political and social barriers: weak institutions, poor governance, corruption, unequal political power, gender inequality, lack of property rights.
How the barriers reinforce one another.
topics.trap: Name the mechanism, not the label. 'Corruption is a barrier' scores little; 'corruption raises the effective cost of investment, deterring FDI and lowering the capital stock' is analysis.

terms.definition: A self-reinforcing pattern in which low income causes low saving and investment, which keeps productivity and income low.
The movement of financial assets out of a country, reducing the funds available for domestic investment.
Reliance on a narrow range of primary commodity exports, exposing a country to volatile prices and adverse terms of trade.
Legally enforceable rights to own, use and transfer assets, without which investment is discouraged.

lesson: Barriers to development reinforce one another, which is why they are so hard to break.
The poverty cycle is the core mechanism: low income means low saving, which means low investment, which means low productivity, which means low income. Nothing in that loop breaks on its own.

Around it sit economic barriers — poor infrastructure, low human capital, dependence on a narrow range of primary exports whose prices swing violently, adverse terms of trade, capital flight, and debt whose interest absorbs the budget. And institutional ones — weak rule of law, corruption, insecure property rights, gender inequality, and conflict.

The examiner's test is whether you name the MECHANISM. Writing that corruption is a barrier earns little. Writing that corruption raises the effective cost of investing, deters foreign direct investment and so holds down the capital stock is analysis, and it is the same sentence length.

topics.title: Economic growth and/or economic development strategies
essentials: Trade strategies: import substitution, export promotion, trade liberalisation, diversification.
Market-based approaches: liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, attracting foreign direct investment.
Interventionist approaches: education, health, infrastructure, industrial policy.
Foreign aid (humanitarian, development, tied), multilateral development assistance, debt relief.
Institutional change: microfinance and mobile banking, women's empowerment, reducing corruption, property and land rights.

lesson: Strategies for development divide roughly into trade, market-based, interventionist and institutional, and none of them works everywhere.

Trade strategies: import substitution builds domestic industry behind protection, which risks permanent inefficiency; export promotion competes in world markets, which demands competitiveness the country may not yet have. Diversification away from primary commodities reduces exposure to price swings.

Market-based approaches — liberalisation, privatisation, deregulation, attracting foreign direct investment — aim to let the price mechanism allocate resources. Interventionist approaches invest directly in education, health, infrastructure and industrial policy. Foreign aid and debt relief can free resources, or entrench dependency and prop up bad governments.

Institutional change is the least glamorous and often the most decisive: property and land rights, reducing corruption, women's empowerment, microfinance and mobile banking that reach people banks never did.

There is no universally best strategy, and saying so is not a cop-out if you say what it depends on: institutional quality, factor endowments, and the stage of development the country has actually reached.
